title: Tenant Egress Rate Limiter (RLS) — Policy & Terraform Spec
author: Leah Nguyen
summary: Design and operational specification for a centralized Tenant Egress Rate Limiting Service (RLS) that enforces per-tenant egress bandwidth and request-rate policies across GPU inference clusters, with Terraform modules, monitoring, and rollout/runbook steps.
content:
Overview:

This document defines the architecture, policy model, Terraform/IaC modules, operational runbook, testing and rollout plan for the Tenant Egress Rate Limiter (RLS). RLS provides enforceable, auditable egress rate and bandwidth controls per tenant (account) across our inference fleet and burst fabric. The target audience is infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who implement tenant isolation, cost controls, and egress SLA guarantees.

Goals:
- Provide per-tenant and per-route rate limits (tokens/sec, max burst bytes) that are enforceable at the network edge and/or NAT egress proxies.
- Integrate with Terraform and our tenant onboarding pipeline so policies can be declared as code.
- Emit metrics and logs for billing reconciliation, SLA reporting, and incident triage.
- Support tiered SLOs (free/dev/paid/enterprise) and emergency shielding for customer-sensitive incidents.

Definitions and Concepts:
- Tenant: Redwood customer account identifier (tenant_id) used across billing and routing.
- Egress policy: A named rate-policy attached to a tenant or tenant+route.
- Token bucket: Enforcement primitive used by the RLS (rate r tokens/sec, burst b tokens).
- Enforcement point: The process/location where an egress decision is applied (edge-proxy, NAT gateway, egress sidecar, or cloud load balancer WAF).
- Global circuit-breaker: Account-level emergency fallback which immediately caps a tenant to a minimal safe rate.

Architecture overview:
- Control plane: Policy API service (internal-only) where RBAC-bound users and CI apply declared policies. Stores policy objects in DynamoDB (or our ConfigStore) keyed by tenant_id and policy_name.
- Sync agent: Periodic pull/push that translates policies to enforcement configs and pushes to edge-proxies or cloud route objects.
- Enforcement plane: Nginx/Envoy egress proxies + iptables token-bucket shim on self-managed NAT pools. For cloud-managed egress we use provider rate-limit objects where supported.
- Observability: Prometheus metrics (ratelimit_allowed, ratelimit_denied, egress_bytes), audit logs (policy change events), and a billing reconciliation export.

Policy model (declarative example):
- Fields:
  - policy_id: string (human name)
  - tenant_id: string
  - scope: [global, region, route]
  - rate_rps: integer (requests per second)
  - bandwidth_bps: integer (bytes per second)
  - burst_bytes: integer
  - sku_tier: [free, dev, standard, enterprise]
  - effective_from / effective_to: ISO timestamps (optional)
  - enforcement_points: list of strings (edge-proxy, nat-pool-a, aws-tgw)
  - tags: list of strings

Sample Terraform YAML snippet (module usage):
```
module "rls_policy_myapp" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra/terraform-modules.git//rls-policy?ref=v1.2.0"

  tenant_id       = "tenant_1234"
  policy_id       = "standard-tenant-default"
  scope           = "global"
  rate_rps        = 200
  bandwidth_bps   = 5_000_000   # 5 MB/s
  burst_bytes     = 10_000_000  # 10 MB burst
  sku_tier        = "standard"
  enforcement_pts = ["edge-envoy-eu", "nat-pool-us-west-2"]
  tags            = ["gpu-inference", "slo:standard"]
}
```

Terraform module outputs (contract):
- policy_resource_id (string) — unique id used by sync agent
- last_apply_sha (string) — commit used for audit
- enforcement_targets (list) — list of endpoints that will receive the config

Enforcement semantics and algorithm:
- Primary primitive: hierarchical token buckets. Tenant-level bucket is checked first, then route-level buckets. If either bucket denies, request is rejected or queued depending on enforcement-point capability.
- Bandwidth accounting uses byte-level tokens for streaming responses; request-rate uses request tokens.
- Grace window: newly-created policies start with a 10-minute grace (soft enforcement) where violations are counted and emitted as metrics but not blocked. This avoids accidental customer impact from IaC mistakes.

SLOs & thresholds (suggested):
- Free tier: 20 rps, 500 KB/s, 2 MB burst (best-effort, excess requests are rejected)
- Dev: 100 rps, 2 MB/s, 8 MB burst (soft throttling preferred)
- Standard: 1000 rps, 10 MB/s, 40 MB burst (strong enforcement, low-latency SLO)
- Enterprise: custom per-contract (configurable via CLI/console and priority queueing)

Observability and metrics (Prometheus tags):
- rls_policy_applied_total{tenant_id, policy_id, enforcement_point}
- rls_rate_allowed_total{tenant_id, policy_id}
- rls_rate_rejected_total{tenant_id, policy_id, reason}
- rls_egress_bytes_total{tenant_id, policy_id, direction}
- rls_policy_sync_latency_seconds

Dashboards & Alerts (recommendations):
- Dashboard: Tenant Overview: per-tenant latency, egress bytes, rejects, and last policy_apply.
- Alert: PolicySyncFail if a policy hasn't been acknowledged by all enforcement_points for > 5m (P2).
- Alert: UnusualRejects if rejects for a tenant spike > 10x baseline in 5m (P1).
- Alert: BillingMismatch if daily egress bytes differ > 3% vs billing export (Finance triage).

Runbook: common incidents and playbook steps:
1) Symptom: Tenant traffic suddenly denied / 503 on inference routes.
   - Check dashboard for rls_rate_rejected_total and policy_sync status.
   - Confirm if a policy change was recently applied (check audit logs last 30m).
   - If within grace window: treat as policy misconfiguration and rollback the Terraform apply.
   - If not: escalate to RLS owners, run steps below.
2) Emergency shielding (fast mitigation):
   - Use rls emergency CLI: `rlsctl shield tenant_1234 --temporary-rate 10` to place tenant into a safe minimal rate. This bypasses per-route blocks and creates a short-lived override (15 minutes).
3) Rolling rollback:
   - Revert the last terraform apply that changed the policy and run `terraform apply -target=module.rls_policy_myapp` in staging, then canary to edge proxy.
4) Long-term fix:
   - Update policy tests, add additional explicit testcases to CI (see Testing section).

Testing strategy (CI/CD):
- Unit: Policy schema validation and invariants (no negative rates, burst limit capped at 10x rate*60s).
- Integration: A local envoy sandbox test that applies the policy via module and then drives synthetic traffic across different routes asserting allow/deny counts.
- Chaos: Periodically run a canary chaos test that injects 10% additional traffic to an internal tenant to verify graceful degradation and alerts.

Terraform/IaC module requirements and constraints (table):
| Input | Type | Required | Notes |
|------|------|----------|-------|
| tenant_id | string | yes | must match tenant registry ID |
| policy_id | string | yes | alphanumeric-dash-only |
| scope | string | yes | global | region | route |
| rate_rps | number | conditional | required for rate policies |
| bandwidth_bps | number | conditional | required for bandwidth policies |
| burst_bytes | number | optional | default = min(bandwidth_bps * 5s, 50 MiB) |
| enforcement_pts | list | yes | map to existing envoy/nat pools |

Operational notes & ownership:
- Team owners: networking-platform@redwood.com (primary), gpu-fleet@redwood.com (secondary).
- Audit and compliance: Every policy change writes an immutable audit event with user, commit sha, and diff. Finance receives a nightly export for billing reconciliation.
- IAM: Only the onboarding CI and designated SREs have write permission to the control plane apply endpoint. Use least-privilege TF service accounts.

Rollout plan (canary phases):
1) Internal-only: deploy RLS in us-west-2 test cluster and validate with synthetic tenants (2 weeks).
2) Beta tenants: opt-in list of internal customers and dev teams (4 weeks) — collect metrics and iterate policy defaults.
3) Gradual ramp: 10% of production egress traffic to enforcement points in us-west-2, 10% in eu-west-1 (4 weeks).
4) Wide rollout: make enforcement default, keep soft-grace for 24h for new policies.

CLI snippets and debug commands:
- Show active policy for tenant: `rlsctl show --tenant tenant_1234 --format json`
- Force re-sync policy to enforcement point: `rlsctl sync --tenant tenant_1234 --point edge-envoy-eu`
- Get recent rejects: `rd-prom-query "sum(rate(rls_rate_rejected_total{tenant_id=\"tenant_1234\"}[5m]))"`

Security and failure modes:
- Threat model: malicious tenant attempting exfiltration via high volume streaming. Mitigation: byte-level enforcement + per-connection caps and connection-level tracking.
- Failure modes: Sync agent crash (policy drift), enforcement point OOM (egress proxy misconfigured), Terraform apply with wrong variables.
- Safe defaults: if enforcement point becomes unreachable, the sync agent enters read-only (no deletes) and health-checks escalate to oncall.

Appendix A — Example incident timeline (realistic exercise):
- 10:03 UTC: Synthetic spike causes Tenant A rejects; dashboard alert fires.
- 10:05 UTC: SRE uses shield CLI to restore minimal operations.
- 10:10 UTC: Audit shows a recent policy apply by CI; rollback performed and new canary applied.
- 10:40 UTC: Metrics stabilize; ticket created for policy/test gaps.

Appendix B — Implementation checklist for module owners:
- [ ] Schema validation unit tests added to module repo.
- [ ] Sync agent acknowledgment handshake implemented (ACK/NAK).
- [ ] Prometheus metrics instrumented and dashboard templates committed.
- [ ] IAM roles and TF service account documented and reviewed.
- [ ] Emergency shield CLI tested and RBAC locked down.

Contact and escalation:
- Primary oncall: networking-platform rotation (see oncall schedule).
- Secondary: gpu-fleet team pager.
- For billing disputes: finance-billing@redwood.com.
